title: Observational Equivalence of LLM and Human Annotation
authors: Kentaro Nakamura; Jing Ling Tan; George Yean

blocks: Observational Equivalence of LLM and Human Annotation∗
Kentaro Nakamura† Jing Ling Tan‡ George Yean§
Last Updated: October 30, 2026
Abstract

In this paper, we show that humans and large language models (LLMs) are observationally equivalent in coding texts. Recent LLMs agree with attentive humans at rates comparable to those observed among humans, and cross-LLM disagreement concentrates on texts that also divide humans. We demonstrate these patterns through replications of text-classification tasks from 14 peer-reviewed political science studies, with 13 LLMs, three human coders (Ph.D. students), and 165 crowd coders, independently applying identical codebooks. We further find that clarifying an underspecified codebook increases agreement among humans and between humans and LLMs. Together, these findings point to ambiguity in texts and coding rules as a shared source of disagreement and challenge the presumption that human labels should take precedence whenever humans and LLMs differ. We therefore argue that the central challenge of text annotation is not simply choosing between humans and LLMs, but developing coding rules that minimize ambiguity and accounting for the ambiguity that remains. To this end, we propose using cross-LLM disagreement to identify difficult cases, guide human review, and refine codebooks, and we develop ambiguity-aware bounds for downstream inference without requiring ground truth for every text.
Keywords: large language models, automated text analysis, Text-as-Data, AI

1 Introduction

Large language models (LLMs) are changing quantitative text analysis by applying natural-language instructions directly to raw text. Earlier text-as-data methods typically relied on dictionaries, bag-of-words representations, or parametric models that abstracted away from how people interpret language (Grimmer and Stewart, 2013; Grimmer et al., 2021, 2022). Because these methods were generally regarded as imperfect approximations of human reading, researchers commonly validated automated annotations against hand-coded labels, treating disagreements as algorithmic errors. LLMs challenge this human-centered validation paradigm. By incorporating definitions, examples, and contextual information into a single prompt, researchers can instruct LLMs to apply codebooks in ways that resemble human annotation. This raises two fundamental questions: Can LLMs annotate texts as reliably as human coders, and what does their performance imply for how researchers should conduct and validate quantitative text analysis?

In this paper, we evaluate LLM-based annotation by replicating binary text-classification tasks from 14 peer-reviewed political science studies. For each study, 13 LLMs, three human coders (Ph.D. students with training in political science), and crowd workers independently classify the same texts using identical codebooks, allowing direct comparison of LLM–human and human–human agreement. We find that, except for an older, weaker model, recent LLMs agree with humans at rates comparable to those among humans themselves. Across studies, LLM–human agreement closely tracks human–human agreement: LLMs agree more with humans when human agreement is higher, and less when it declines.

We further find that disagreement among different annotators is systematically concentrated in the same texts. When humans disagree about a text, LLMs and crowd-sourced workers also exhibit substantially greater disagreement, although crowd workers’ overall agreement with humans is substantially lower than that of LLMs. These patterns point to a common source of disagreement: ambiguity in the text or coding rule rather than errors specific to any one type of annotator. Consistent with this interpretation, clarifying an underspecified codebook substantially reduces disagreement among humans and sufficiently capable LLMs.

These findings change how disagreement should be interpreted. When an LLM disagrees with a human coder, the disagreement should not automatically be treated as model error, because human coders are often divided on the same cases. Instead, disagreement can reflect ambiguity in the text or coding rule rather than a failure unique to the LLM. Under the same instructions, sufficiently capable LLMs agree with humans at rates comparable to those among humans themselves, leaving little empirical basis for preferring attentive human coding on annotation quality alone. Moreover, disagreement across LLMs and between LLMs and humans is informative: it tends to concentrate on texts that also divide attentive human coders, providing a useful signal of ambiguity. Validation should therefore ask not only whether an LLM reproduces a human label, but also whether the text and coding rule yield a stable classification.

Building on this reinterpretation, we propose a practical workflow for LLM-based text annotation. Researchers should first develop a clear codebook and manually apply it to a small random sample to identify common ambiguities and refine coding rules. They should then verify that candidate LLMs can reliably apply the codebook and use disagreement across suitable LLMs to identify additional borderline cases for targeted review before annotating the full corpus. Because some ambiguity may remain, we develop ambiguity-aware bounds that use cross-LLM disagreement as a scalable proxy for residual ambiguity, allowing downstream inference without assuming a uniquely defined ground-truth annotation for every text.

This paper makes two contributions. First, a longstanding annotation literature argues that disagreement among attentive humans can reveal ambiguity in texts or coding tasks rather than simply reflecting coding error (Aroyo and Welty, 2015; Uma et al., 2021). We extend this insight to LLM-based annotation, showing that cross-LLM disagreement provides an informative, scalable signal of ambiguity rather than model failure. Second, building on existing human–LLM annotation workflows (Dunivin, 2025; Meng et al., 2024; Pangakis and Wolken, 2025; Xiong et al., 2025; Yuan et al., 2025), we propose using cross-LLM disagreement to select which texts humans review, so that review effort targets the cases most likely to reveal ambiguities in the

codebook. We further develop ambiguity-aware bounds that account for residual ambiguity in downstream inference without requiring a uniquely defined target annotation for every text, an assumption common in methods for bias correction in downstream inference using LLM-generated annotations (e.g., Angelopoulos et al. 2023; Carlson and Dell 2025; Egami et al. 2023, 2024; Fong and Tyler 2021; Nakamura 2025; Zrnic and Cand`es 2024).
2 Paradigms of Quantitative Text Analysis: Before and After LLMs
2.1 Goal and Philosophy of Text Annotation

The goal of content analysis is to make “replicable and valid inferences from texts (or other meaningful matter) to the contexts of their use” (Krippendorff 2018, p.24). In this respect, coding text is not different in kind from measurement elsewhere in social sciences. In the conceptual model of measurement proposed by Adcock and Collier (2001), researchers first have a background concept, the broad constellation of meanings associated with a term such as “democracy” or “security”, and then formulate it into a systematized concept, the specific formulation the researcher adopts for a given study. The operationalization needs to track the systematized concept (validity) and be reproducible by different humans (reliability).

Text annotation is a special case of exactly this process, but what makes text unique is its unstructured and high-dimensional nature. By unstructured, we mean that the concept of interest is not directly observed. Instead, it must be inferred from language. As Krippendorff (2018) emphasized, texts have no “reader-independent” qualities: their meaning is not contained in words but is brought to them by readers. Thus, two careful coders can read the same passage differently, not because one has made an error, but because text genuinely admits multiple interpretations. High dimensionality compounds this problem. As a corpus grows, the space of possible textual configurations grows with it, continually producing borderline and outlier cases (Grimmer et al., 2022). The ambiguity that enters at the operationalization stage therefore cannot be fully eliminated in many cases, no matter how carefully the codebook is written.

This also points to an inherent tension between reliability and validity. One could push annotation toward the structured-data ideal by operationalizing a concept as a mechanical, easily replicated procedure, such as counting occurrences of a keyword. Such rules are trivially replicable, but they typically sacrifice validity to the systematized concept (Kracauer, 1952). Moving in the opposite direction, i.e., toward more holistic human judgment, improves validity but lowers reliability as it leaves more to the reader. Any codebook that is at once usable and valid thus retains some irreducible ambiguity, and that ambiguity is distributed unevenly across a corpus: some texts are read the same way by everyone, while others are genuinely contestable.

Taken together, these features imply that text annotation is a demanding task even for humans, and that there is no ground truth to be recovered for some cases. Indeed, a large body of literature has recognized that inter-coder reliability among attentive human coders is rarely perfect because of ambiguity, raising questions about whether a unique ground truth exists (e.g., Aroyo and Welty 2015; Mikhaylov et al. 2012; Plank 2022; Pavlick and Kwiatkowski 2019; Uma et al. 2021).
What researchers can do is narrow the range of defensible readings through operationalization and validate the measurement repeatedly (Krippendorff, 2018).
2.2 Text-as-Data before Large Language Models

Automated text analysis addresses a problem of scale: corpora such as news articles and party manifestos often exceed what humans can annotate by hand. Automated methods extend systematic content analysis by translating human-defined concepts into reproducible computational procedures.

Before LLMs, automated text analysis relied on dictionary approaches, topic models, and supervised classifiers (see Grimmer and Stewart 2013 for a review). Yet these methods do not explicitly model the data-generating processes underlying text production or human interpretation (Grimmer et al., 2021). Accordingly, Grimmer and Stewart (2013) argue that automated text-analysis algorithms “use insightful, but

wrong, models of political text to help researchers make inferences from their data” (p.270) and “will never replace careful and close reading of texts” (p.268). Researchers therefore evaluated automated methods primarily by their agreement with human judgments (Hase, 2022), interpreting high agreement as evidence of accuracy and low agreement as algorithmic error or bias.

Researchers also used crowdsourced workers to construct validation sets (e.g., Budak et al. 2016; Park 2021; Plank 2022; Rheault et al. 2019; Theocharis et al. 2016; Ying et al. 2022). Crowd workers offered a less expensive alternative to experts, but their annotations were generally noisier because they tended to have less training, expertise, and incentive to attend carefully to the task (Benoit et al., 2016; Snow et al., 2008). Nevertheless, their annotations were typically presumed more informative about textual meaning than automated outputs. This human-centered paradigm was reasonable before LLMs, when human annotations were assumed to approximate textual meaning more closely than any algorithm could.
2.3 Text-as-Data after Large Language Models

LLMs can now perform tasks that, until recently, were thought to require sophisticated reasoning: they pass graduate examinations, solve competition-level mathematics problems, and score competitively on multitask language-understanding benchmarks (Hendrycks et al., 2021; Rathje et al., 2024). If these systems can handle such hard tasks, are we still confident that they cannot perform text annotation as humans do?

Due to its importance, recent years have seen extensive validation of LLM annotation (e.g., Gielens et al. 2026; Gilardi et al. 2023; Goodall et al. 2026; Halterman and Keith 2026; Heseltine and Clemm von Hohenberg 2024; Liu and Sun 2025; Rathje et al. 2024; T¨ornberg 2025; Yang et al. 2025; Ziems et al. 2024; Zhu et al. 2023), but existing evaluations provide mixed evidence. Several studies find that LLMs outperform human annotators on tasks such as relevance, topic, and frame classification (Heseltine and Clemm von Hohenberg, 2024; T¨ornberg, 2025). Other research documents substantial variation across tasks and models (Gong et al., 2026; Ziems et al., 2024). In political science, Halterman and Keith (2026) show that LLMs can struggle to follow political-science codebooks that operationalize complex, researcher-defined constructs. On the other hand, Gilardi et al. (2023) found that early LLMs agreed with ground truth generated by human annotations more often than crowd-sourced workers.

A fundamental difficulty with interpreting these results is that the truth is generally unobserved in reality. Most existing evaluations compare model outputs with a human-coded reference and implicitly treat human labels as ground truth.1 Such comparisons can establish whether an LLM reproduces a particular set of human labels, but they cannot distinguish among three possibilities: that the LLM is wrong, that the human label is wrong, or that the text and coding rule admit multiple defensible interpretations. The last possibility is especially important for text, because even attentive humans may disagree when language or coding rules are ambiguous. Indeed, a growing literature questions whether human annotations should automatically be treated as an error-free gold standard (e.g., Bisbee and Spirling 2026; Clark et al. 2021; Hosking et al. 2024).

In this paper, rather than treating human annotations as ground truth, we assess whether LLMs and attentive human coders are observationally equivalent under a common coding framework (i.e., holding fixed the explicit operationalization and task information available to them). We evaluate this equivalence from two perspectives. First, we examine whether LLM–human agreement approaches the agreement observed among humans themselves. Second, we examine whether texts that generate disagreement among human coders also exhibit greater LLM–human and LLM–LLM disagreement. If both patterns hold, then disagreement with any single human label is less naturally interpreted as an error specific to the LLM and may instead reflect difficulty or ambiguity in applying the common coding rule.

In social science, the construct of interest is typically latent, so validation cannot generally proceed by comparing a measure with the ground-truth. Instead, the measurement literature views validity as an accumulation of evidence supporting the intended interpretation of a measure (Grimmer et al., 2022; Lowe and Benoit, 2013; Messick, 1995; Quinn et al., 2010), and human coding provides one such source of evidence as it has long served as a substantively grounded operationalization of researcher-defined concepts. Accordingly, if LLM annotations correspond to human annotations to approximately the same degree that humans correspond to one another, and if both types of coders struggle with the same texts, this provides validity-relevant evidence that LLMs preserve similar substantive information under the specified operationalization.
2.4 Testable Hypotheses
Our argument yields four sets of predictions. First, if recent LLMs apply a common coding rule as reliably as humans, their agreement with humans should approach the agreement observed among humans.
Hypothesis 1 (Reliability). Recent LLMs achieve agreement with human coders comparable to the agreement observed among human coders themselves.
Second, if annotation disagreement reflects ambiguity in the text or codebook, the same observations should generate disagreement across different annotators.
Hypothesis 2-a (Human disagreement). LLM–human disagreement is greater for texts on which human coders disagree with one another.
Hypothesis 2-b (LLM disagreement). Disagreement across LLMs is greater for texts on which human coders disagree with one another.
Third, if disagreement arises from ambiguities, clarifying the codebook should improve agreement across annotators.
Hypothesis 3 (Clearer codebook). A revised codebook increases agreement among humans and between LLMs and humans.

Finally, the same relationship between textual ambiguity and disagreement should extend to crowdsourced coders. However, because crowd coders have less incentive to pay attention, we expect their annotations to correspond less closely with human annotations than LLM annotations do.
Hypothesis 4-a (Crowd disagreement). Disagreement among crowd-sourced coders is greater for texts on which humans disagree or LLM outputs vary across models.
Hypothesis 4-b (LLMs versus crowd coders). LLMs achieve greater agreement with human coders than crowd-sourced coders do.
3 Replication Studies by LLMs and Humans
3.1 Procedure

Data Collection: We focus on recent applications of automated text analysis in leading political science journals. We selected 13 articles using text classification from the American Journal of Political Science, the American Political Science Review, and the Journal of Politics from 2018 through 2025. To ensure broad substantive coverage, we included three studies in American politics (Feltovich and Giovannoni, 2024; Gilardi et al., 2021; Lacombe, 2019), four in international relations (Clark and Dolan, 2021; Mattingly et al., 2025; Schub, 2022; Thrall, 2025), and six in comparative politics (Blaydes et al., 2018; Blumenau and Lauderdale, 2018; Bush and Clayton, 2023; Jung, 2020; Parthasarathy et al., 2019; Osnabr¨ugge et al.,

2021). We further include Arias (2022) as a theoretically hard case. Recent work suggests that LLMs may struggle to classify concepts rare or absent from their training data (Halterman and Keith, 2026), so findings from general-interest journals may not fully generalize to specialized subfields. Arias (2022) provides a demanding robustness check because it examines climate securitization, a construct unlikely to appear frequently in LLM training corpora and difficult to define even within international relations scholarship (Buzan et al., 1998; Phillis et al., 2018).

For each study, we selected one concept and drew a simple random sample of 100 texts from its original corpus. These texts were independently annotated by LLM and human coders. Appendix S2.1 describes concept selection and summarizes the studies.

Codebook / Prompt generation: For each paper, we construct a standardized codebook template to ensure consistency across papers. The template consists of seven components: (1) role assignment, (2) topic definition, (3) paper and data description, (4) category definition, (5) classification rules, (6) label wording, and (7) step-by-step reasoning instructions. We design this template based on the prompt engineering literature for large language models (e.g., Atreja et al. 2024; Halterman and Keith 2026; Mu et al. 2024; Weber and Reichardt 2024). We then generate the paper-specific components (2)–(6) based on the descriptions in the article with the help of LLMs (GPT-5.5). For each component, we check the generated content against the corresponding descriptions in the published paper and revise it when necessary. This procedure standardizes codebooks across studies (see Appendix S2.3 for the detailed procedure). While our main analysis uses the prompt containing all components, we also check how much the results would change by systematically varying prompts (see Appendix S4.1.2).

One limitation of our research design is the codebook quality. Because we are not experts on all 14 studies, our codebooks are based solely on descriptions in the original articles. This reflects a tradeoff between replicating many studies for broader external validity and the limited availability of published codebooks. Appendix S1.2 therefore replicates the same analysis procedure using three papers with original, more detailed codebooks and confirms that our main findings hold under these codebooks as well.

LLM Annotation: We then annotate each text using 13 different LLMs that span a wide range of parameter counts, developers, release dates, and likely training data. Seven are open-weight models: Mistral 7B (Jiang et al., 2023), LLaMA 3.1-8B (Grattafiori et al., 2024), Qwen2.5-7B and Qwen2.5-14B (Qwen Team, 2024), Gemma 3-12B and Gemma 3-27B (Gemma Team et al., 2025), and GPT-OSS-20B (OpenAI et al., 2025). The remaining six are proprietary API models: three from the GPT-5 family (GPT-5.4 mini, GPT-5.4, and GPT-5.5) and three from Anthropic (Claude Haiku 4.5, Claude Sonnet 4.6, and Claude Opus 4.6). Table 1 lists each model with its release date.

Human Annotations: Finally, the three authors of this paper, who are Ph.D. students with training in political science, independently annotated the same texts using the same codebooks as the LLMs, without discussing difficult cases or consulting external information. We avoided calibration and reconciliation discussions because these could introduce task-specific information or shared interpretations not explicitly documented in the codebook and thus unavailable to LLMs. Requiring both human and LLM annotators to follow the same explicit coding instructions allows us to directly compare LLM–human and human–human agreement under a common coding framework.
We assessed human intercoder reliability using Krippendorff’s α (Krippendorff, 2018), which measures agreement among multiple coders while adjusting for chance agreement. Formally,
Observed within-text disagreement α := 1 − Baseline disagreement from the label distribution.
Thus, α = 1 indicates perfect reliability and α = 0 indicates chance-level agreement. α can be negative when observed disagreement exceeds that expected by chance.

Across these exercises, we find no systematic evidence that disagreement with the original annotators or subject-matter specialists exceeds disagreement among our three human coders. These results support the use of our human annotations as a reasonable benchmark for evaluating LLM annotations.

3.2.2 Disagreement Concentrates in Texts That Divide Humans

To test Hypothesis 2-a, we use a leave-one-human-out procedure. For each text, we classify it as clear when two humans agree and as ambiguous when they disagree. We then evaluate each LLM against the remaining held-out human, repeating the procedure for all three choices of held-out human and averaging the results.

Figure 2 shows that LLM agreement declines sharply on texts that divide humans. Among the studies with higher reliability, agreement with the held-out human, averaged across the 13 models, falls from approximately 0.89 on clear texts to 0.66 on ambiguous texts. Among the studies with lower reliability, it falls from approximately 0.81 to 0.65. These results support Hypothesis 2-a. LLM–human disagreement is concentrated in the same texts that generate disagreement among humans, implying that much of the disagreement reflects ambiguity in the text or codebook rather than model-specific error. Appendix S3 also provides illustrative examples of these contested texts.

3.2.3 Clarifying the Codebook Improves Agreement

Finally, we test Hypothesis 3 using the classification task from Schub (2022). Specifically, we developed a revised codebook that goes beyond our standardized template by providing clearer definitions, more explicit inclusion and exclusion rules, and guidance for mixed cases. The three humans and 13 LLMs then reclassified the same texts using the revised instructions.

Figure 3 shows that the revised codebook raises human–human agreement from approximately 0.27 to 0.64. It also increases LLM–human agreement for most recent models, several of which reach between 0.54 and 0.64 and approach the human benchmark. The improvement is not uniform, however. Mistral-7B and Qwen2.5-7B perform worse under the more detailed instructions, suggesting that a clearer but more complex codebook may be difficult for weaker models to apply consistently. Together, these findings show that improving the codebook can increase agreement among humans and between humans and recent capable LLMs.

3.2.4 Same finding for Crowdsourced Workers, but they are less reliable than LLMs

Finally, we extend our analysis to crowdsourced annotation. We recruited 165 U.S. participants through Cloud Research Connect and randomly assigned each participant to one of the 14 papers we used in replication or to the revised codebook version of Schub (2022) analyzed in the previous section. For each paper, we limited the coding task to 20 texts to reduce respondent fatigue while retaining enough observations for analysis. Specifically, we selected the 10 texts with the highest agreement across LLMs and the 10 texts with the lowest agreement to sample both easy and difficult cases. Participants were asked to apply the same codebook used in the previous section to annotate the assigned texts. To reduce potential LLM-assisted responses, we disabled copying and pasting and implemented multiple bot-detection and data-quality checks. We detail the annotation procedure in Appendix S2.6 and preregistered hypotheses, results, and robustness checks in Appendix S4.2.

We obtain two main findings. First, we find that crowd workers exhibit greater disagreement on ambiguous texts, regardless of whether ambiguity is measured by disagreement among LLMs or among humans. The difference in Gini impurity between ambiguous and non-ambiguous texts is both statistically and substantively significant: Gini impurity is 14 percentage points higher for the texts with the lowest versus highest LLM agreement and 10 percentage points higher for texts on which humans split versus those on which they reached unanimous agreement (Figure 4).

Second, we find that human–human and LLM–human agreement both decline for lower-reliability tasks, whereas crowd–human agreement remains consistently lower (Figure 5). This extends Gilardi et al. (2023) by comparing intercoder agreement without presuming human labels are ground truth. Most strikingly, LLM–human agreement closely tracks agreement among humans across both types of tasks, which is not the case for crowd-sourced workers.

4 Practical Takeaways

Given these results, we propose a procedure that uses multiple LLMs to efficiently identify borderline cases, refine the codebook, and ultimately conduct honest statistical inference. Figure 6 summarizes the procedure. Below, we explain each step in detail.
4.1 STEP 1: Generate a clear codebook

The first step is to construct a codebook. Researchers should first define what they want to measure and how to operationalize it. This step is consequential, as our results show that much apparent annotation error, whether by LLMs or humans, is ambiguity introduced during operationalization. While the best codebook depends on the setting and concept of interest, clear classification rules generally improve LLM agreement with human annotations (see Appendix S4.1.2). Researchers should state the classification rules clearly and revise them through trial and error in STEP 2.
4.2 STEP 2: Test codebook with LLMs / humans and inspect disagreements

Before annotating the full corpus, researchers should manually code a small simple random sample to assess how often the codebook yields clear classifications and identify common weaknesses. Drawing on their substantive understanding, they should review disagreements and difficult cases and revise the codebook. This step evaluates the codebook rather than the annotator and is necessary regardless of who performs the full annotation.

Next, researchers should apply the revised codebook to multiple LLMs across additional subsets for further pilots. They should expand human review by targeting texts on which LLMs disagree, rather than additional random texts, because these cases are more likely to reveal remaining codebook ambiguity.2

Researchers should review these cases and refine the codebook until clearer instructions no longer resolve disagreements, following iterative human-review approaches in the literature (Dunivin, 2025; Pangakis and Wolken, 2025; Xiong et al., 2025).

Because model capabilities evolve rapidly, we recommend pilot-based selection rather than fixed models or prompts. Ideally, multiple humans should annotate a small subset. Exclude models whose LLM– human agreement falls substantially below human–human agreement, since their disagreement may reflect limited capability or poor instruction following rather than ambiguity. In our studies, recent medium- and large-scale models perform similarly and open-source models perform comparably to proprietary state-of-the-art models, consistent with the literature (e.g., Yang et al. 2025). Once the codebook is clear, we find that prompting technique, such as role assignment, contribute relatively little to agreement compared with explicit classification rules (Appendix S4.1.2).
4.3 STEP 3: Account for residual ambiguity

Once the codebook has stabilized, researchers can annotate the full corpus. Nevertheless, some texts may remain ambiguous even under well-developed codebooks (Aroyo and Welty, 2015), as our replications illustrate. Forcing these texts into a category (for example, coding all unclear cases as zero) may increase agreement while compromising validity. Residual ambiguity may therefore distort estimates and inference in downstream analyses, such as regressions.

5 Conclusion

Using replications of 14 political science papers, we evaluate LLM-based annotation by comparing annotations from 13 LLMs, three human coders (Ph.D. students with training in political science), and 165 crowd-sourced workers applying identical codebooks. We find that recent LLMs agree with humans at rates comparable to those among humans themselves, establishing an observational equivalence between LLM and human coding. We further show that this equivalence arises because different annotators struggle with the same texts: LLM–human disagreement concentrates in texts that divide humans, and cross-LLM disagreement is substantially greater on those same cases. Clarifying an underspecified codebook reduces disagreement among humans and sufficiently capable LLMs. Crowd-sourced workers exhibit the same ambiguity-related pattern, although their overall agreement with humans is substantially lower than that of recent LLMs.

Because humans and LLMs often disagree on the same borderline cases, divergence from human labels need not indicate model error. Researchers should therefore prioritize conceptualization and codebook development, using cross-LLM disagreement to identify difficult cases and refine coding rules. Because some ambiguity may remain, we develop ambiguity-aware bounds that do not require a unique ground-truth label for every text. Reliable text analysis requires capable annotators, careful operationalization, and statistical inference that explicitly propagates residual ambiguity rather than treating it as ordinary annotation error.

blocks: S1 Validating our Research Design

Our main analysis compares annotations produced by LLMs and the three authors of this paper under standardized codebooks. This section examines whether our findings depend on the use of standardized codebooks or annotations produced by the authors of this paper. To address these concerns, we compare our annotations with external expert annotations and extend our analysis to studies with original expert-developed codebooks.
S1.1 Validation of Human Coding Against External Benchmarks

The three human coders in our main analysis are the authors of this paper, rather than subject-matter experts in all of the substantive domains examined. We therefore conduct two supplementary comparisons to assess how closely our annotations correspond to the annotations made by domain-specific experts.

Comparison with source-author annotations. First, we compare our annotations with the original human annotations from the three replicated studies whose coders classified the same binary concept that we code: Feltovich and Giovannoni (2024), Lacombe (2019), and Schub (2022). Consistent with the premise of this paper, we do not treat the original expert annotations as a gold standard. Instead, we ask whether the original annotators behave like additional members of our coding panel. Specifically, for each text, we compute the share of disagreeing pairs among (i) the three pairs formed by the original annotation and each of our coders and (ii) the three pairs of our own coders. Within each study, we then estimate the mean difference between (i) and (ii) across texts, together with its 95% confidence interval. If our human coding departs systematically from the original expert coding, for example because of differences in the coding instructions or expertise, disagreement with the original annotations should be significantly higher than disagreement among our coders, making the difference estimates positive. Because we developed a revised codebook for Schub (2022), we report results under both our original and revised codebooks.

Figure S1 reports the results. Across all three studies, we find no evidence that disagreement between our human coders and the original expert annotations is greater than disagreement among our human coders themselves. For Feltovich and Giovannoni (2024), Lacombe (2019), and Schub (2022) under the revised codebook, the two disagreement rates are nearly identical (the difference is almost zero by point estimates) and not statistically significantly different. For Schub (2022) under the original codebook, the estimated difference is even negative, indicating that our human coders agree with the expert annotations more often than they agree with one another. Overall, these results provide no indication that our human annotations differ from the original expert annotations beyond the level of disagreement observed among our own human coders, supporting the use of our human annotations as a reasonable benchmark.

Comparison with subject-matter specialists. Because the original studies provide only a single reference label per text, the comparison above can reveal whether our coders diverge from expert annotations, but cannot show how much experts disagree with one another or whether their disagreements are concentrated on the same texts as those of other coders.

We therefore recruited two subject-matter experts for Arias (2022) and three for Clark and Dolan (2021), all holding Ph.D. degrees in political science and working and/or publishing in areas corresponding directly to the topics of each paper. Each independently annotated the same 20 texts used in our crowd-sourced study, comprising the 10 texts with the highest and with the lowest Gini impurity across LLMs, following the same codebooks as our coders, crowd workers, and LLMs. For these texts, we examine disagreement both within and across four groups: subject-matter experts, our coders (attentive non-experts), crowd workers, and LLMs. This design allows us to examine two questions. First, does the level of disagreement among subject-matter experts differ systematically from that among other annotator groups (our coders, crowd workers, and LLMs)? Second, does disagreement across all four groups concentrate on the same texts, as would be expected if it also reflects ambiguity in the text and coding rule that expertise does not resolve?

Table S1 presents the results. For texts with low cross-LLM disagreement (Panel A: Agree stratum), experts agree with one another 93% of the time, and agreement within and between our human coders and LLMs is similarly high. In contrast, crowd workers exhibit substantially lower agreement rates. For texts with high cross-LLM disagreement (Panel B: Disagree stratum), however, expert–expert agreement declines sharply, from 93% to 60%, closely mirroring the declines in human–human and LLM–LLM agreement. Agreement between experts, our coders, and LLMs also declines substantially. Interestingly, we do not observe a comparable decline in within-group agreement among crowd workers, whose agreement remains relatively low in both strata.

These findings provide further evidence that annotation disagreement reflects shared difficulties in interpreting texts and applying coding rules, even among subject-matter experts. Importantly, cross-LLM disagreement identifies texts that also divide experts, suggesting that it can serve as an effective tool for identifying difficult cases. Thus, our main findings also appear to extend beyond our three human coders to subject-matter experts.
S1.2 Validation Using Original Expert-Developed Codebooks

Another concern with our replication design is the quality of the codebooks used. Our main analysis uses codebooks developed through a standardized procedure because most published studies do not make their original coding instructions available. Although this approach facilitates comparisons across studies, our reconstructed codebooks may not preserve all substantively important distinctions in the original coding schemes. It therefore remains unclear whether our findings generalize to tasks using more detailed, expert-developed codebooks.

We next examine whether our finding that LLM–human disagreement concentrates on texts that divide humans also holds under these original codebooks. We first replicate the leave-one-human-out analysis in Section 3.2.2 using our three human coders. For each text, we hold out one human coder and classify the text as clear when the remaining two humans agree and as ambiguous when they disagree. We then calculate each LLM’s agreement with the held-out human separately for clear and ambiguous texts. We repeat this procedure for each of the three choices of held-out human and aggregate the results. The procedure is identical to Section 3.2.2 except that we used the detailed, expert-developed codebook.

Figure S3 presents the results. Consistent with our main analysis, many recent LLMs exhibit substantially lower agreement with a held-out human on texts where the other two humans disagree. This pattern appears across the three validation studies, despite their differences in substantive content, number of classification categories, and coding instructions. The magnitude of the difference varies across models, with weaker models not always exhibiting the same pattern. These findings provide additional evidence that LLM–human disagreement is concentrated on texts that also generate disagreement among human coders, even when using detailed coding instructions developed independently of our main replication procedure.

In sum, these validation studies provide additional support for our main findings. The reliability of our human coders is comparable to that of the original human coders in the two studies where individual original annotations are available. Moreover, recent LLMs can achieve substantial agreement with human annotators under independently developed codebooks, although their relative performance varies across tasks. Most importantly, cross-LLM disagreement is systematically associated with disagreement among both our human coders and the original human annotators. Thus, our main finding that human and LLM disagreement reflects common difficulties in applying coding rules does not appear to be driven solely by the standardized codebooks constructed for our primary analysis.
S2 Details of Replication Studies
S2.1 Summary of Each Study (Main Paper)

For each of the 14 main replication studies, we selected one concept for text classification. When a study examined multiple concepts or topics, we selected the one most closely related to its substantive findings. If multiple concepts were equally relevant, we randomly selected one among them.

In this section, we summarize the paper, the text corpus used, the topics into which those texts are classified, how the topic classification is used in the original analysis, and the topic of interest in our reanalysis. We also report the summary of text classification tasks in Table S3.

Arias (2022), Who Securitizes? Climate Change Discourse in the United Nations. Arias asks why some states frame climate change as a security issue in the United Nations, and which states are most likely to make such securitizing moves. The paper argues that securitization is shaped by agenda-control incentives: P5 states benefit from moving issues toward the Security Council, while highly vulnerable states such as SIDS may resist losing agenda control. Empirically, the paper finds that UN climate discourse overall is not securitized, P5 states are more likely to securitize climate change, and SIDS are less likely to do so. The text data are speeches by state representatives in the UN General Assembly General Debate, filtered to speech segments discussing climate change. The analysis uses 4,525 climate-related speech segments from 1,987 speeches, with the earliest climate-related speech segment appearing in 1984.

Blaydes et al. (2018), Mirrors for princes and sultans: advice on the art of governance in the medieval Christian and Islamic worlds. The paper compares medieval Christian and Islamic political advice texts (“mirrors for princes”) to examine how ideas of governance evolved across regions. Using text-as-data methods, it identifies shared thematic structures and tracks their evolution over time. It finds broad similarities across traditions but key divergences, including declining religious emphasis in Europe and shifting ruler-centered discourse in the Islamic world. The data consist of translated medieval political advice texts addressed to rulers in Christian Europe and the Islamic world. These texts include guidance on governance, morality, religion, and social order, often written by elites for kings, courts, or political audiences.

Blumenau & Lauderdale (2018), Never let a good crisis go to waste: Agenda setting and legislative voting in response to the EU crisis. Blumenau and Lauderdale study how the 2008 global financial and sovereign debt crises affected agenda setting and legislative voting in the European Parliament. They argue that crises weaken legislators’ attachment to the status quo, allowing pro-integration agenda setters to pass more integrationist policy than would otherwise have been possible. Empirically, they show that crisis-related votes increasingly divided MEPs along the pro- versus anti-European integration dimension rather than the left-right dimension. The text data are European Parliament legislative summary texts linked to roll-call votes from the sixth and seventh European Parliaments, covering 2004-2014. These summaries describe the purpose, background, and content of legislation under discussion, and are used to identify whether votes concern crisis-relevant financial and economic policy areas.

Bush & Clayton (2023), Facing Change: Gender and Climate Change Attitudes Worldwide. The article argues that the gender gap in climate concern widens with national wealth because men in richer countries perceive greater costs from climate mitigation. The text analysis draws on open-ended survey responses, collected in an original ten-country survey, in which respondents describe the personal consequences they associate with acting on climate change. A structural topic model recovers recurring topics – among them denying any personal cost, anticipating higher taxes or prices, and pointing to environmental benefits. The topics are used at the response level, with the prevalence of each estimated directly as a function of respondent gender and national income. We reanalyze the material-costs topic, which most directly operationalizes the paper’s proposed mechanism.

Clark & Dolan (2021), Pleasing the Principal: U.S. Influence in World Bank Policymaking. The paper examines how World Bank policy conditionality reflects the preferences of powerful states, especially the United States. It shows that countries politically aligned with the U.S. receive fewer and less stringent policy conditions. The mechanism is primarily indirect, with World Bank staff designing programs consistent with U.S. preferences rather than explicit bargaining. The data consist of World Bank Development Policy Financing (DPF) loan conditions from 2005–2018, including detailed text and categorical coding of policy requirements. Each observation captures policy conditions (prior actions) imposed on borrowing countries as part of loan agreements.

Feltovich & Giovannoni (2024), Campaign Messages, Polling, and Elections. The article examines how candidates’ track records and campaign messaging jointly affect voter welfare, pairing a formal model with a laboratory experiment. The texts are campaign messages written by experimental subjects playing incumbent and challenger politicians in repeated elections. Coders classify each message along five dimensions that may co-occur: positive self-promotion, negative campaigning against the opponent, claims about one’s own competence, claims about past performance, and promises about future performance. These message-level labels are used directly as dependent variables in regressions on the experimental conditions. We reanalyze negative campaigning, the behavior behind the paper’s sharpest prediction – that challengers attack incumbents more as incumbent performance worsens.

Gilardi et al. (2021), Policy Diffusion: The Issue-Definition Stage. The paper studies policy diffusion at the issue-definition stage, asking whether prior smoking-ban adoptions in other U.S. states predict how later states frame the issue. Using structural topic models, it finds that prior adoptions predict practical, observable frames such as rules, enforcement, bars and restaurants, casinos, and local legislation, but not normative frames such as freedom. The paper concludes that diffusion shapes policymaking before adoption by affecting how issues are publicly defined. The data are newspaper paragraphs about anti-smoking laws from 49 newspapers covering 49 U.S. states between 1996 and 2013. The final corpus contains 52,675 relevant paragraphs after broad keyword retrieval and filtering with crowd annotation and machine-learning classification.

Jung (2020), The Mobilizing Effect of Parties’ Moral Rhetoric. The article asks whether parties’ use of moral rhetoric mobilizes their own supporters. The texts are party manifestos from six English-speaking democracies (Australia, Canada, Ireland, New Zealand, the United Kingdom, and the United States), drawn from the Comparative Manifesto Project and divided into quasi-sentences. Each quasi-sentence is classified as moral or non-moral adapting from the Moral Foundations Dictionary, which flags language invoking concerns such as care, fairness, loyalty, authority, and sanctity. These document-level labels are not used directly: they are aggregated to the manifesto level as the share of moral quasi-sentences, which serves as an independent variable predicting copartisan turnout. We reanalyze the moral/non-moral distinction itself, the construct on which the paper’s entire argument rests.

Lacombe (2019), The Political Weaponization of Gun Owners. Lacombe studies why the NRA has been unusually effective at mobilizing gun owners and influencing U.S. gun politics. The paper argues that the NRA cultivated a politicized gun-owner social identity through long-term membership communications and programs, then used perceived threats to that identity to mobilize political action. The conclusion is that this identity-based mobilization is an important, often overlooked channel of interest-group power. The paper analyzes two original text corpora: NRA American Rifleman editorials from 1930-2008 and gun-control-related letters to the editor from four major U.S. newspapers: the New York Times, Arizona Republic, Atlanta Journal-Constitution, and Chicago Tribune. The newspaper letters are ordinary citizens’ public arguments about gun control, excluding elites and NRA officials.

Mattingly et al. (2025), Chinese State Media Persuades a Global Audience. The article shows, through a nineteen-country survey experiment, that exposure to Chinese state media moves global audiences toward

seeing the “China model” as superior to the American one. The text analysis characterizes the messaging itself, using the descriptions of videos published by China’s CGTN and the United States’ ShareAmerica. A topic model sorts these descriptions into topics, grouped by the authors into portrayals of China’s political model (responsive institutions, competent leadership, and Western dysfunction) and its economic model (poverty alleviation, infrastructure, and trade and innovation), alongside other news and cultural content. The topics are used in aggregate, as corpus-level proportions that describe typical state-media messaging and motivate the choice of representative videos used as experimental stimuli; they do not enter a regression. We reanalyze the Western-dysfunction topic, the most clearly defined and substantively interpretable of the individual topics from our reading.

Osnabrugge et al. (2021), Playing to the Gallery: Emotive Rhetoric in Parliaments. The paper studies when and why politicians use emotive rhetoric in parliamentary debates. It argues that emotive rhetoric is strategically deployed to appeal to voters, especially when speeches reach a broader public audience. Using large-scale data from UK and Irish parliaments, it finds that high-profile debates (e.g., Prime Minister’s Questions) feature significantly more emotive language. The data consist of nearly one million parliamentary speeches from the UK House of Commons (2001–2019) and a comparable dataset from the Irish Parliament. These are formal legislative speeches delivered in different types of debates that vary in public visibility and audience size.

Parthasarathyetal et al (2019), Deliberative Democracy in an Unequal World. The data are verbatim transcripts and translations of 50 village assembly meetings held on Republic Day 2014 in rural Tamil Nadu, India. Each document is an uninterrupted speech, with speaker gender and position identified; the full corpus contains 1,736 speeches from gram sabha proceedings. A text should be labeled Yes for fund allocation when Discussion of government funds, budgets, allocations, or rupee amounts.

Schub (2022), Informing the Leader: Bureaucracies and International Crises. The paper examines how bureaucratic position shapes the information advisers provide to leaders during international crises. Using over 5,400 advisory texts from U.S. Cold War crises, it argues that bureaucratic specialization affects informational content and uncertainty rather than policy preferences. Foreign policy bureaucracies emphasize political attributes of adversaries and express greater uncertainty, whereas military bureaucracies emphasize military characteristics. The data consist of internal U.S. foreign policy deliberation texts during Cold War international crises, including memoranda, NSC discussions, presidential advisory meetings, and FRUS documents. The corpus contains adviser-level speech acts from senior officials across bureaucracies such as the State Department, Defense Department, CIA, NSC, and Joint Chiefs of Staff.

Thrall (2025), Informational Lobbying and Commercial Diplomacy. The paper examines how informational lobbying shapes bilateral diplomacy, arguing that diplomats prioritize issues emphasized by the interest groups supplying them with information. Using the expansion of American Chambers of Commerce abroad and oral histories from U.S. diplomats, the paper shows that diplomats exposed to active AmChams devote greater attention to commercial diplomacy. The findings suggest that business interests influence foreign policy by subsidizing diplomats’ information environment rather than through coercive lobbying. The paper uses approximately 1,500 oral history interviews conducted with retired U.S. diplomats by the Association for Diplomatic Studies and Training (ADST). The interviews describe diplomats’ experiences across embassy postings worldwide from roughly the 1940s–2000s, including discussions of trade, investment, security, human rights, and bilateral relations.

S2.2 Summary of Each Study (Validation Studies in Appendix S1.2)

This section summarizes the three studies used in the validation analyses in Appendix S1.2. For each study, we describe the original research and text data, the annotation procedure and coding instructions, and the classification task reproduced in our reanalysis. All three validation studies use 100 randomly sampled texts with original study’s human annotations.

Benoit et al. (2016): Benoit et al. (2016) examine whether non-expert crowd workers can reproduce expert assessments of political parties’ policy positions. Using 18,263 sentences from the Conservative, Labour, and Liberal Democrat manifestos across six British general elections, the authors compare policy positions estimated from crowd-sourced annotations with those derived from expert coding. They find that aggregated crowd annotations closely approximate expert estimates of parties’ economic and social policy positions.

The original annotation procedure consists of two steps. First, coders classify each sentence as primarily concerning economic policy, social policy, or neither. Second, sentences classified as economic or social are placed on a five-point left–right scale. The authors provide detailed coding instructions in Appendix Section 6, which were administered to both experts and crowd workers. The expert annotations were produced by six coders, comprising three of the paper’s authors and three PhD students in politics at New York University.

In our reanalysis, we use the original sentences as the unit of classification, providing the two preceding and two following sentences as context, consistent with the original crowd-coding procedure. We randomly sample 100 sentences from the 5,444 sentences annotated by all six expert coders. We focus on the first classification task, assigning each sentence to one of three categories: economic policy, social policy, or neither. BFRS Dataset on Political Violence in Pakistan (Bueno de Mesquita et al. 2015; Halterman and Keith 2026). The BFRS Political Violence in Pakistan Dataset, originally developed by Bueno de Mesquita et al. (2015), documents 28,731 incidents of political violence in Pakistan between 1988 and 2011. The dataset covers a broad range of violent events, including assassinations, terrorism, riots, violent political demonstrations, and attacks involving state and non-state actors. The original data were collected by researchers at Lahore University of Management Sciences, who systematically reviewed newspaper reports from the Lahore edition of The Dawn. Human coders identified incidents of political violence and recorded their characteristics, including the type of violence, location, perpetrators, and consequences. Each incident was also accompanied by a short narrative summary. The original researchers additionally conducted a reliability assessment using independent coding by a separate research team.

More recently, Halterman and Keith (2026) adapted the BFRS dataset to evaluate whether LLMs can apply detailed political science codebooks. Because the original newspaper articles were unavailable, they use the English-language event summaries written by the original BFRS annotators as classification inputs. They restructure the original coding instructions into a 12-category, single-label classification task. Each category is accompanied by a definition, clarification and exclusion rules, and illustrative examples. The task requires assigning each event to one category, such as assassination, terrorism, riot, or violent political demonstration.

In our reanalysis, we randomly sample 100 event summaries from the adapted dataset for which original human-coded labels are available. We retain the 12-category classification task and use the detailed codebook developed by Halterman and Keith (2026), making only minimal adjustments to the required output format for LLM annotation. We compare our annotations with the original BFRS human-coded event labels. Unlike the other two validation studies, however, the available BFRS data contain only one reference label per event. Consequently, we cannot directly measure agreement among the original human coders.
S2.3 Details of Codebook Generation

Because most of the replicated studies do not publish the codebooks used in their original annotation, we construct a codebook for each study from the descriptions in the published article, using GPT-5.5 (accessed through ChatGPT) as a drafting aid. We first read each article in full to understand the concept of interest and how it is used in the analysis. We then upload the article as a PDF to GPT-5.5, together with the prompt below, and ask the model to draft the paper-specific components of the codebook. Finally, we check every generated component against the article and revise any content that is inaccurate, incomplete, or inconsistent with how the original authors define and use the concept. Thus, every component of the final codebooks has been verified against the source article. The prompt is as follows:

We are developing a prompt for an LLM to classify texts used in a political science paper. I have attached the paper as a PDF. Our goal is to classify whether a text should be categorized as category name as defined and used in the paper’s analysis. Please create a high-quality prompt for this task. Specifically, I want you to provide the following components:
Definition: Provide a definition of the target category in no more than 10 words. Whenever possible, base the definition on how the concept is used in the attached paper.
Classification rules: Provide a classification rule of no more than 10 words for each of the following:
when the label should be Yes, when the label should be No, and what kinds of cases are tricky or borderline.

Label wording: Provide five keywords and related expressions for the target category. Include alternative label names, synonyms, and close paraphrases when they are semantically relevant. Keep this concise while covering the major cases.
Summary of the paper: Provide a summary of the paper in no more than three sentences, covering the research question, context, and main findings.

Summary of the data: Provide a summary of the text data in no more than two sentences. Describe the source and context of the texts (e.g., speeches in the United Nations General Assembly or parliamentary speeches in India). Focus on the data itself rather than how it is analyzed.”

S2.6.2 Text selection and Data Quality

For each coding task we selected 20 texts from the replicated papers, taken verbatim.4 Out of the original 100 texts per paper used in our main analyses, we used stratified sampling to obtain the 10 “most agreed” and 10 “most disagreed” texts based on the LLM annotation. In other words, for each paper, we took the 10 texts with highest LLM disagreement (ranked by across-model Gini impurity) and 10 texts with lowest disagreement, calculated using the original 10 LLMs (excluding the three Claude models, which were added to our analysis after the crowd-sourced experiment). This oversamples ambiguous texts by design, so that every task spans both straightforward and difficult cases and lets us compare coders across that range. For all analyses involving crowd annotations, we only use the annotations from the subsample of 20 texts per task, from crowd workers, humans, and LLMs.

Of note, Schub (2022) contributes one set of 20 texts, coded under both its original and its improved codebook. Holding the same set of 20 texts constant allows us to compare the effects of the codebook change since assignment to each task is randomized. Across the 14 papers, our text selection procedure yields 280 unique texts.

We capped each task at 20 texts to protect response quality and potential declines in data quality if the task was too long. We estimated the number of texts to assign for crowd coding based on the expected duration of the task, informed by our own human coding and a pilot test. In our pilot test of N = 42 fielded shortly before the main study (also in June 2026 and on Connect with the same demographic selection and tasks), coding 20 texts took a median of 10.7 minutes and mean of 11.3. We found this to be short enough to hold a coder’s attention while still giving enough texts to compare coders within a task. Our main survey took a median of 12.8 minutes and mean of 14.8. For all tasks, text order is randomized to reduce fatigue and learning effects.

Given that our analysis compares human crowd workers with LLMs, we took extensive care to prevent AI-assisted responses (Westwood, 2025). First, we programmed our survey on Qualtrics to prevent any copying and pasting of text content, raising the barrier to routing a text through an LLM. Second, we added a honeypot text field that is visible to bots but not to humans. Third, we enabled Qualtrics’ bot-detection features, a CAPTCHA question, and duplicate-submission prevention.5 Fourth, our survey provider, CloudResearch Connect, applies its own extensive anti-bot screening.6

We used our pilot to test the survey’s length and data quality checks before fielding the main study. We generally found high data quality and good engagement across both the pilot and full survey: crowd agreement with the humans is fairly high, completion times are close to what we expected, and straight-lining is rare. The final sample of 165 respondents includes only those that pass every preregistered exclusion criteria. Numerous respondents failed our attention checks and are excluded while one respondent took more than eight hours and is excluded for exceeding Connect’s maximum survey time. Respondents are pre-screened on Connect for native English language proficiency and a platform approval rate of at least 95%, so we do not collect any data from those that do not meet these criteria. Additionally, among our final sample of 165, three respondents straight-lined all twenty answers. Given that we did not preregister straight-lining as an exclusion criterion, we retain these three responses in the main specification and drop them only as a robustness check. S4.1.1 Agreement with Human Majority-Vote Labels

Our main analysis compares each LLM with individual human coders, so that human and LLM annotations are treated symmetrically and LLM–human agreement can be benchmarked directly against human–human agreement. In applied research, however, human annotations are often aggregated, for example by majority vote or adjudication, before being used as a reference for validating automated measures. We therefore examine how LLM–human agreement changes when the human reference is constructed by majority vote. Specifically, for each text, the majority-vote label is defined as the label selected by at least two of the three human coders. Holding the texts, codebooks, and LLM outputs fixed, we calculate Krippendorff’s α between each model’s annotations and the majority-vote labels and compare it with the model’s average pairwise α with the individual human coders.

Figure S5 reports the results for studies with relatively higher and lower human reliability. We find that majority voting increases LLM–human agreement regardless of which group is aggregated. Individual LLMs generally agree more closely with the human majority-vote labels than with individual human coders. Similarly, the majority vote across LLMs achieves higher agreement with individual humans than the

average individual LLM. Relative to average pairwise LLM–human agreement, majority voting across LLMs increases Krippendorff’s α by 0.07 on average, while majority voting across humans increases it by 0.08. These similar gains suggest that part of the disagreement between LLMs and humans reflects variation across individual annotators, which can be reduced through aggregation in either group. Importantly, greater agreement does not necessarily imply more accurate annotations, since majority voting may override substantively defensible minority interpretations.
S4.1.2 Within-Model Annotation Stability under Prompt Variation

Our main replication analysis holds the prompt fixed, using a single structure built from six components (role, topic definition, classification rules, label wording, paper and data description, and a reasoning cue; see Table S4). This lets us compare models and studies on common ground, but raises a concern: we do not know how much our conclusions reflect this particular prompt rather than the task itself. To probe this, we toggle each component on or off to generate all 26 = 64 prompts per paper and run them through seven open-source LLMs (Mistral 7B, LLaMa 3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen2.5-14B, Gemma 3-12B, Gemma3-27B, GPT-OSS-20B). We test whether this sensitivity reflects substantive ambiguity rather than arbitrary instability, by asking whether prompts disagree most on the texts that humans also find hard to code. The fully specified prompt, with all six components included, is our reference point and we refer to it as prompt 64.

The analysis uses all the 64 prompts applied to texts by each model. We measure within-model prompt disagreement using Gini impurity, which equals zero when all 64 prompts produce the same classification and reaches its maximum of 0.5 when the prompts are evenly divided between labels 0 and 1. We then compare this prompt disagreement between texts on which all three human coders agree and texts on which at least one human assigns a different label. Because human reliability varies across studies, we report the comparison separately for relatively higher reliability studies, defined by human Krippendorff’s α > 0.4, and relatively lower reliability studies, defined by α < 0.4. For each model and reliability group, the table reports the mean Gini impurity for human-agreement texts and human-disagreement texts, their difference, and the p-value from a two-sample comparison of the corresponding text-level Gini values.

Table S10 shows that within-model prompt disagreement is generally higher for texts on which humans disagree. This pattern is statistically significant for both Gemma3 models, Llama3.1 (8B), both Qwen2.5 models, and GPT-OSS (20B) in both reliability groups. The largest increases among Higher Reliability studies are 0.124 for GPT-OSS (20B) and 0.108 for Qwen2.5 (7B); for GPT-OSS (20B), the increase is 0.122 among Lower Reliability studies. Overall, the results indicate that prompt sensitivity often tracks human-defined ambiguity, although the strength and direction of this relationship vary across models.

S4.1.3 Within-Model Annotation Stability under Stochastic Decoding

Our main analysis identifies ambiguous texts using disagreement across different LLMs. However, most applied researchers often use a single model rather than a panel of models. We therefore examine whether repeated runs of the same model provide a useful within-model measure of annotation uncertainty. For each of the seven open-source LLMs, we classify the same 100 texts from each of the 14 studies ten times under stochastic decoding with temperature 1.0. For each model–text pair, we define instability as an indicator equal to one if the predicted label changes at least once across the ten runs. We then summarize the prevalence of instability by study and model and compare it between texts on which the humans agree and texts on which they disagree.

Figures S7 and S8 show that within-model instability is generally greater in the more difficult studies, but its magnitude varies substantially across models. LLaMA 3.1-8B and GPT-OSS-20B exhibit the greatest instability overall, followed by Mistral-7B, whereas the Gemma 3 and Qwen2.5 models produce substantially more stable annotations. Table S11 further shows that instability is concentrated on texts that divide humans for GPT-OSS-20B (0.406 versus 0.112), LLaMA 3.1-8B (0.308 versus 0.131), and Qwen2.5-14B (0.060 versus 0.010). All three differences are statistically significant. By contrast, the corresponding differences are small and statistically indistinguishable from zero for Mistral-7B, both Gemma 3 models, and Qwen2.5-7B. These results provide partial support for stochastic-decoding instability as a within-model proxy for ambiguity: it identifies texts that divide humans for some models, but its informativeness depends substantially on the model.

S4.2 Additional results for Crowd Sourced Annotation

This section elaborates on the results from the crowd-sourced annotation, which affords a blinded, preregistered test of the paper’s central claims. This section proceeds with reporting the results from the preregistered hypotheses for the experiment, followed by robustness checks, and alternative measures of intercoder agreement.
S4.2.1 Preregistered Hypotheses

We preregistered six hypotheses that extend the paper’s theory from human and LLM coders to a third set of coders: crowd workers. Among the six, three confirmatory hypotheses restate the paper’s core predictions for the crowd.

• H1 (text difficulty): When LLMs agree with one another, crowd-sourced workers are more likely to agree with each other. In other words, the Gini impurity of LLMs is correlated with that of crowdsourced workers. This maps on to the main paper’s Hypothesis 4a that disagreement reflects textual ambiguity rather than coder identity.

• H2 (crowd vs. LLM agreement with humans): The average agreement of crowd-sourced workers with three humans (authors’ coding) is lower than that of LLMs with three humans. In other words, the average LLM-human agreement is significantly higher than the average crowd-human agreement. This maps on to the main paper’s Hypothesis 4b: LLMs align with humans better than crowd coders.

• H3 (codebook improvement): Using an improved codebook decreases the Gini impurity among crowd-sourced workers (H3a) and increases the average agreement of crowd-sourced workers with humans (H3b). We test this on the original and improved Schub (2022) codebooks over the same 20 texts. This maps on to the main paper’s Hypothesis 3: clearer coding rules reduce disagreement.

We further probe three exploratory hypotheses on coder-and-text level sources of agreement as moderators. We preregister these as exploratory hypotheses given these analyses involve slicing an already small sample size. A full copy of our preregistered hypotheses, research design, and analysis plan are available on OSF, at https://osf.io/5wp2k.

• H4 (coder knowledge): We test whether crowd–human agreement is higher among workers with higher baseline knowledge of politics/policy.(H4a), higher frequency of political news consumption, (H4b), or higher education levels (H4c).
• H5 (coder attention): We test whether crowd–human agreement is higher on texts workers spend longer on (H5a) or on shorter texts (H5b).

• H6 (text heterogeneity): Crowd Gini impurity is lower on less contested texts than on more contested ones, with strata defined by LLM disagreement (H6a) or human unanimity (H6b). This maps on to the main paper’s Hypothesis 4a, similar to H1 but contrasting texts across strata.

For all survey results, we use the 20-text-per-paper survey sample described in Appendix S2.6. Because this subsample oversamples contested texts by design, agreement and reliability levels on it are generally lower than in the full corpus. We conduct multiple hypothesis testing for the three confirmatory hypotheses (four tests: H1, H2, H3a, H3b) using the Benjamini–Hochberg correction. We report the summary of findings for each hypothesis in Table S15. Below, we walk through each result in turn.

S4.2.6 Robustness to Quality Checks and Exclusions

We conducted a series of robustness checks to address the threat of AI use in survey research (Westwood, 2025). In our preregistration and Section S2.6, we applied a set of inclusion/exclusion criteria to screen for our final sample of 165: (1) we sample only from respondents who indicated English as a native language on Connect, given the difficulty of the task; (2) we automatically screen out respondents that fail any of our attention or bot checks; (3) we sampled only from respondents with an approval rate of 95% or more (Peer et al., 2014; Kennedy et al., 2020); (4) We exclude respondents that exceed a maximum time spent of 48 minutes (Connect’s default maximum time) and drop any duplicate responses that are identical to others. Ultimately, we removed one respondent that exceeded the maximum time and found no respondents with duplicate responses across all questions; the other exclusions are automatic screens on Connect and Qualtrics.

Besides the above preregistered exclusions, we conducted robustness checks with two additional filters: we dropped respondents that straight-line all text classification responses (answered all 20 texts as “Yes” or all as “No”) and those that score below 0.5 on Qualtrics’ CAPTCHA scores. Both checks are soft exclusions given that they do not lead to a respondent being screened out based on our preregistration but they nonetheless raise data quality concerns and we thus remove them sequentially and rerun our main analyses without those responses.

A key advantage of our ambiguity-aware bounds is that the estimand retains a clear substantive interpretation: it is the range of downstream quantities consistent with all substantively defensible classifications of the ambiguous texts. This differs from approaches that propagate disagreement among coders as statistical uncertainty. For example, the quasi-Bayesian procedure proposed by Egami et al. (2024) repeatedly samples one of the human annotations for each text, re-estimates the downstream quantity, and pools the resulting draws. Such an approach is appropriate when disagreement represents uncertainty about which annotation should be used for an otherwise well-defined target. It does not, however, resolve the form of ambiguity considered here, in which multiple classifications are substantively defensible and no unique annotation is defined. Averaging over those classifications instead defines a new quantity that depends on how competing interpretations are weighted. Our bounds avoid imposing such weights and instead characterize the full range of downstream results consistent with the defensible classifications.
S5.2 Empirical Application

We finally illustrate the ambiguity-aware bounds by revisiting Arias (2022), in which a text-based measure serves as the outcome of a linear regression. This paper asks which states frame climate change as a security issue in the United Nations, a process known as climate securitization. The study argues that securitization follows agenda-control incentives: P5 states (Permanent members of the United Nations: China, France, Russia, United Kingdom, United States) benefit from moving climate change toward the Security Council, whereas highly vulnerable states such as Small Island Developing States (SIDS) may resist such a shift because it would reduce their agenda control. The outcome underlying this claim is constructed from text, because each climate-related speech segment must be classified as securitizing or not. We revisit this application because, as our replication shows, the concept of securitization is demanding even for attentive human coders. Some segments, such as those invoking existential harm without referring to security institutions, remain genuinely ambiguous (Table S9).
Following the original analysis, we estimate the linear probability model
Yi = β1 P5c(i) + β2 SIDSc(i) + XT c(i),t(i)γ + δt(i) + εi, (S3)

where Yi is the true securitization label of segment i, delivered by country c(i) in year t(i). For genuinely ambiguous segments, this label may be undefined. The vector Xc,t contains country-level controls, including public concern about climate change, democracy, experienced climate disasters, changes in average temperature, voting affinity with the United States, military expenditure, logged GDP per capita, and logged population, and δt denotes year fixed effects.

To implement the bounds, we first develop a codebook and conduct an independent human review of a simple random sample of 200 segments.7 To develop the codebook, one of the three authors reviewed the relevant literature on climate securitization and formulated the coding rules.8 Using this codebook, all three authors independently recorded both a binary classification and whether the codebook left a substantively defensible alternative classification for each segment. Finally, the author who conducted the literature review independently reclassified all segments for which at least one of the three authors identified ambiguity or for which the initial binary classifications disagreed. In the end, 24 texts are classified as ambiguous.

Next, we annotate all 4,525 segments using seven open-weight LLMs (Mistral 7B, LLaMA 3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen2.5-14B, Gemma 3-12B, Gemma 3-27B, and GPT-OSS-20B) using the updated prompt introduced in Appendix S2.4. For comparison, we consider two benchmark approaches. First, we estimate the original regression using the majority vote of the LLM annotations as the outcome, without accounting for ambiguity. Second, we apply design-based supervised learning (DSL; Egami et al. 2024), treating the majority vote of the human annotations as the ground-truth label. DSL corrects for measurement error in LLM annotations, but it does not accommodate fundamental ambiguity in the classification task because it assumes that each text has a uniquely defined gold-standard label.

Figure S13 compares the ambiguity-aware bounds with the naive LLM regression and DSL. Both benchmark approaches yield substantially more precise estimates because they impose a unique label on every text and therefore do not account for conceptual ambiguity in the annotation task. These results underscore the importance of developing a precise operationalization and translating it into a clear codebook. Researchers should resolve avoidable ambiguity through substantive refinement of the coding rules before turning to statistical adjustment. The ambiguity-aware bounds are designed for the ambiguity that remains after this process, making explicit the extent to which the substantive conclusion depends on unresolved borderline cases.
